The question "Is sitting the new smoking?" is contested, with genuinely conflicting research outcomes and expert opinions. On one side, Dr. James Levine of the Mayo Clinic claims "sitting is more dangerous than smoking, kills more people than HIV, and is more treacherous than parachuting," and some medical experts argue that the health risks of prolonged sitting are comparable to those of smoking [d3, d4]. A physician at NewYork-Presbyterian also states that "the cumulative damage of sitting for prolonged periods of time, over several years, can be equated to the negative health consequences of smoking," affecting every organ system [d6]. Research cited by Runner's World further suggests that sitting increases risk of death and disease even for those who exercise regularly, drawing an explicit analogy to smoking as an independent risk factor [d5].

On the other side, an international team of researchers published in the American Journal of Public Health concluded that "sitting is not the new smoking," noting that smoking increases the risk of premature death by approximately 180%, compared to only 10–20% for excessive sitting [d10]. A peer-reviewed analysis in PubMed/PMC similarly found that "the mass-media enthusiasm for condemning sitting by making comparisons to smoking has far outpaced the available scientific evidence," with risk estimates for smoking far outweighing those for sitting [d1]. Healthline reports that the relative risk of death for smokers is 2.80 (men) versus only 1.22 for sitting, and that quitting smoking increases life expectancy far more than reducing sitting time [d9]. Some researchers also argue that sitting itself is not the problem—rather, physical inactivity is, and 60–75 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous daily activity can reverse the effects of sitting 8 hours a day [d11, d8].
